sources.locator: React Learn and Reference; React 19.2; provisions applicable to Lists and stable keys
sources.claim: React list keys identify sibling items across renders so reconciliation preserves the intended component and DOM state.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Render a list with `items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} ... />)`. The **key** tells React which item each row belongs to across renders. When the list is sorted, filtered or has items inserted, React matches old and new rows **by key**, so each row keeps its own DOM and state, like typed text or focus. Use a **stable, unique id from the data**. The array **index** is only safe when the list never reorders, inserts or deletes; otherwise state sticks to the position instead of the item. Keys must be unique among siblings, not globally.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Each to-do row has a small notes input. A learner types "buy milk" into the note for "Shopping", then sorts the list by date. The note text stays in the first row, which is now "Homework". The list used `key={index}`. A todo list uses stable todo.id while sorting, insertion, and deletion preserve each row's input state. In this lesson you'll render and update a reorderable list while explaining key-based reconciliation.

examples.title: The to-do notes that swapped rows
examples.situation: A todo list uses stable todo.id while sorting, insertion, and deletion preserve each row's input state.
walkthrough: **Bug:** with key={index}, sorting moved titles but left each typed note at its old position.
**Stable todo.id:** switching to `key={todo.id}` lets React move each TodoRow, with its note state, to the new position.
**Test:** type in Shopping's note, sort by date, and a test will find "buy milk" in the input labelled "Note for Shopping".
examples.result: Each note stays with its own to-do through sorting, inserting and deleting.

examples.title: Every row re-mounted
examples.situation: A developer silences the key warning with `key={Math.random()}`. Now every keystroke anywhere makes all inputs lose focus.
walkthrough: Each render generated new keys for every row.
React saw all old rows as gone and created new ones, losing focus and state.
Fix: use the item's stable id.
examples.result: Typing keeps focus, and rows are only created or removed when items really are.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Array index is always the best key because it is unique during one render.
misconceptions.correction: Keys must also be stable across renders. An index describes a position, so when items are reordered, inserted or removed, state follows the position instead of the item. Use a stable id from the data.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The to-do notes that swapped rows", where did the typed note end up after sorting?

analogy.example: Keys are like **name tags on people in a queue**. If people shuffle and you track them by name tag, each keeps their own bag (state). If you track them by position ("person 1", "person 2"), the bags stay in place and end up with whoever steps into that spot.
limitations: People notice lost bags; React silently hands state to the wrong row.
Random keys = new name tags every minute: nobody is recognised.

farTransfer.prompt: Build a reorderable list (move up/down buttons) where each row has an editable input. Write tests that type in a row, move it, and assert the text moved with it; then show the failure with index keys.

remediation.explanation: For every map ask: **If this list is sorted, filtered or edited, does each key still point to the same item?** If not, use a stable id from the data.

recap.summary: To render and update a reorderable list, map items to elements with a key that is unique among siblings and stable across renders, such as the item's id. React reconciles rows by key, so each row keeps its own state through sorting, insertion and deletion; index and random keys break that.
